subject: english-language-and-literature
title: English Language and Literature MYP 5 eAssessment Paper C (3 tasks, 80 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1.1 | A 2]]
Task 1: Analysing
Questions 1.1 to 1.4 focus on the key concept of communication. Question 1.5 focuses on the key concept of connections. The criteria assessed are A (Analysing) and B (Organizing). Suggested time for Questions 1.1 to 1.4: 15 minutes. Suggested time for Question 1.5: 35 minutes.

Text A: 'The Quiet Quarter' (a short story extract, written for this paper)
This extract is from a story set in a city where citizens' conversations are measured by wall-mounted meters.

On Verity Street the meters hummed all day, a low green note that Kiri had stopped hearing years ago, the way you stop hearing your own heartbeat. Every doorway had one: a small white box with a dial, its needle trembling between CALM and CONCERN. Nobody spoke above the green.

Kiri's mother taught her the code before she could read. Two fingers on the wrist meant danger. A tapped temple meant listen. A hand pressed flat against the chest meant I love you, which was the only sentence nobody had ever managed to ban, because nobody could hear it.

That morning, walking to the water depot, Kiri found a bird. It was a sparrow, brown and ordinary, wedged in the grating of the pavement, and it was singing. Not the polite chirp of the loudspeaker birds that piped out of the lamp-posts every dawn, but a ragged, joyful, off-key song that climbed the brick like ivy.

The needle on the nearest meter shivered. Moved. Crossed into amber.

Kiri knelt. Her heart beat so loud she was certain the whole street could count it. The sparrow tilted its head at her, and for the first time in her life she thought: it is not the noise that is dangerous. It is the listening.

Somewhere behind her, a door unlocked.

She did not look round. She pressed a hand flat against her chest, and the sparrow sang on.

Text B: a graphic-novel page (written for this paper; in the live exam this would be an illustrated page)
Title of the graphic novel: 'Static'. Page 14. Four panels, described in words.

PANEL 1 (wide, top of page). A grey city skyline seen from a rooftop. Every window is a rectangle of television light, all the same blue. A boy, Jonah, in a hooded jacket sits at the edge of the roof with his back to us. Caption (yellow box, top left): "Everyone I know is watching the same thing."

PANEL 2 (small, square). Extreme close-up of Jonah's face, lit by the screen of a small handheld radio. One eye only is shown, wide and bright. Sound effect, jagged letters curving across the panel: KSSSHHH-krrk. Speech bubble with a wobbly outline, from the radio: "...anyone... out there...?"

PANEL 3 (small, square). A tall, thin figure in a white coat stands on the roof behind Jonah, casting a long shadow across the page. The figure's face is blank, with no features. A thought bubble, with small circles leading to Jonah's head, contains only: "!"

PANEL 4 (wide, bottom of page, no border). The full-page background turns completely black. In the centre, small white letters: "I turned the dial. I will not turn it back." The bottom corner of the panel is torn, as if the page is breaking.

Q 1.1 Comment on the use of the sound of the meters in the first paragraph of Text A. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies the meters' sound without explaining, e.g. the meters hum all day. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): comments with some explanation, e.g. the 'low green note' that Kiri 'had stopped hearing' shows constant surveillance has become normal, and the simile of the heartbeat shows how deeply it is part of her. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.2 | A 3]]
Refer to Text A (printed in Question 1.1). Explain the effect of the sentence 'it is not the noise that is dangerous. It is the listening.' (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies an effect without development, e.g. it shows Kiri has a new thought. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes an effect with some explanation, e.g. the contrast of 'noise' and 'listening' shifts the blame from the sparrow to the system of surveillance. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): explains the effect consistently with quotation, e.g. the two short parallel sentences, the pause of the full stop and the structure 'not X... It is Y' deliver a moment of revelation, so the reader sees Kiri's first act of independent thought and the story's theme that authority, not freedom, is the true threat. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.3 | A 3]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Analyse the effect of the sound effect and speech bubble in Panel 2. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a feature with no development, e.g. there is a noise from the radio. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes the effect with some justification, e.g. the jagged lettering of KSSSHHH-krrk shows the poor signal and suggests tension. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): analyses the effect consistently with precise reference, e.g. the curving, jagged sound effect makes the reader hear the interference, while the wobbly outline and broken ellipses in '...anyone... out there...?' suggest a faint, fragile human voice, so the audience feels the loneliness and hope of contact outside the controlled world. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.4 | A 2]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Describe the purpose of the final panel. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a purpose without explanation, e.g. it ends the page. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes a purpose with an example, e.g. the black borderless background and torn corner show that the safe world has broken, and the small white text with Jonah's words reads as a decisive vow, leaving the reader eager to see the consequences. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.5 | A 10 | B 10]]
Refer to Text A and Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Compare and contrast how the two texts present individuals who resist control. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)

Criterion A (Analysing) is worth 10 marks and Criterion B (Organizing) is worth 10 marks.
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A (10 marks) and Criterion B (10 marks), 20 marks in total. Criterion A (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for effective, perceptive analysis of content, language, structure and technique in both texts with extensive, well-chosen evidence; 6 to 8 for considerable analysis with sufficient, relevant evidence; 3 to 5 for adequate analysis with some evidence; 1 to 2 for limited analysis with few or no examples. Indicative content: Text A (third-person, past tense, limited viewpoint): setting of surveillance through the meters and colour (green, amber); code gestures; the sparrow as symbol of natural freedom contrasted with the 'loudspeaker birds'; simile ('like ivy'); the quiet, understated resistance of the flat hand on the heart; a final line of open tension ('a door unlocked'). Text B (graphic novel, first-person caption): visual conformity (identical blue windows), the radio as lifeline, onomatopoeia, the faceless figure as a symbol of authority, shadow, panel size and the borderless black final panel; direct declaration of choice ('I will not turn it back'). Contrast: small, silent, emotional rebellion vs a decisive, active turn of the dial; subtle suggested threat vs visually looming threat; language-led vs image-led. Similarity: both end on moments of commitment and both use symbols of communication (bird, radio). Award up to [10] for Criterion A. Criterion B (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for effective organisation: clear structure, comparison and contrast sustained throughout, effective linking and a conclusion; 6 to 8 for a considerable degree of organisation with sustained comparison; 3 to 5 for an adequate degree of organisation with some comparison; 1 to 2 for limited organisation, with the texts mostly treated separately. Indicative content: a clear thesis in the introduction; thematic paragraphs (e.g. the control system, the symbols of freedom, the resistance); explicit comparison words; precise integrated references to both texts; a conclusion that evaluates how form shapes the portrayal. Award up to [10] for Criterion B.

questions.content:
[[Q 2.1 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 2: Producing literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of creativity. The criteria assessed are C (Producing text) and D (Using language).

Image 1 (described in words): a vast field of sunflowers at the end of a hot day, all facing the same direction except one, which has turned its head toward the camera. A rusty bicycle leans against a fence post at the edge of the field.
Image 2 (described in words): a narrow stairwell in an old building. Each step is worn in the middle. A coat has been left on the bannister. At the top of the stairs a door stands slightly open, and a bar of white light spills out onto the dark wood.

Using one of the images, write a short story or the opening of a story, in which a character makes a decision that changes their life. You may consider purpose, characterisation, setting, mood and point of view. State which image you are using before you start. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion C (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for a high degree of insight and imagination, perceptive stylistic choices and extensive precise detail; 6 to 8 for considerable insight and imagination, thoughtful choices and sufficient detail; 3 to 5 for some insight and imagination, some stylistic choices and some detail; 1 to 2 for limited insight, few stylistic choices and little detail. Indicative content: a named image integrated into setting or plot; a clearly motivated character and a believable moment of choice; tension and a controlled narrative arc; symbolism (the one sunflower, the open door); a purposeful ending. A response that uses neither image nor the prompt scores 0 for C. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): 9 to 10 marks for an effective range of vocabulary and sentence structures, consistently suitable register and high accuracy with only minor errors; 6 to 8 for a varied range, considerable accuracy and errors that do not hinder communication; 3 to 5 for an adequate range, a degree of accuracy and errors that sometimes hinder communication; 1 to 2 for a limited range, with errors that often hinder communication. Indicative content: a deliberate narrative voice, varied sentence lengths, precise verbs, figurative language, consistent tense, and accurate punctuation and paragraphing. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.

questions.content:
[[Q 3.1 | B 10 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 3: Producing non-literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of communication. You will create a piece of non-literary writing in relation to the global context scientific and technical innovation: digital life and the impact of technology on communities.

Your school is considering a plan to issue every student with a tablet and replace printed textbooks and exercise books. Write an article for the school magazine giving your view on whether this plan is a good idea. The criteria assessed are B (Organizing), C (Producing text) and D (Using language). (Approximately 350 words) (30 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion B (10 marks): organisation suited to a magazine article: headline, optional standfirst, engaging opening, logical paragraphs for each argument or counter-argument, and a conclusion; 9 to 10 effective, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 adequate, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion B. Criterion C (10 marks): perspective on technology in communities shown through insight, relevant detail and examples (access, distraction, equity, environment, handwriting, learning); 9 to 10 high degree of insight and extensive detail, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 some, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): register suited to a school-magazine readership, varied sentence structures, a clear authorial voice and sensible use of persuasive devices (rhetorical question, anecdote, balanced contrast), with accurate grammar and punctuation; 9 to 10 high accuracy and effective register, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 a degree, 1 to 2 minimal. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.
